But this is not the true calf love. That comes with the down upon the lip. People laugh at "calf love," but one might as well laugh at the wonder of dawn or the coming of spring. When David Copperfield fell in love with the eldest Miss Larkins, he was really in love with the opening universe, and the eldest Miss Larkins happened to be the only available lightning conductor for his emotion.

The important thing is that you should contract "calf love" while you are young. It is like the measles, which is harmless enough in childhood, but apt to be dangerous when you are grown up. The "calf love" of an elderly man is always a disaster. Hence the saying, "There's no fool like an old fool." An elderly man should not fall in love. He should walk into it. He should survey the ground carefully as Mr. Barkis did. That admirable man took the business of falling in love seriously:

"'So she makes,' said Mr. Barkis, after a long interval of reflection, 'all the apple parsties, and does all the cooking, do she?'

"I replied that such was the fact.

"'Well, I'll tell you what,' said Mr. Barkis. 'P'raps you might be writin' to her?'

"'I shall certainly write to her,' I rejoined.

"'Ah!' he said, slowly turning his eyes towards me. 'Well! If you was writin' to her, p'raps you'd recollect to say that Barkis was willin', would you?'"

This is a model of caution in the art of middle-aged love-making. The mistake of the "Northern Farmer" was that he applied the same middle-aged caution to youth. "Doänt thou marry for munny; but goä wheer munny is," he said to his son Sammy, who wanted to marry the poor parson's daughter. And he held up his own love-making as an inspiration for Sammy:

And I went wheer munny wor, and thy moother coom to and Wi' lots o' munny laäid by, and a nicetish bit o' land. Maybe she worn'd a beauty: I nivver giv' it a thowt; But worn'd she as good to cuddle and kiss as a lass as an't nowt?

I have always hoped that Sammy rejected his father's counsel and stuck to the poor parson's daughter.

"However, this is not the genuine experience of youthful infatuation. True calf love arises when one feels the first down on their lip. While many might scoff at the notion of "calf love," such jesting is akin to mocking the beauty of dawn or the arrival of spring. When David Copperfield found himself enamored with the eldest Miss Larkins, he was not merely infatuated with her; he was, in fact, captivated by the vast potential of the universe, with the eldest Miss Larkins serving as the sole conduit for his burgeoning emotions.

It is crucial to experience "calf love" during one's youth. Much like measles, this form of affection is relatively harmless in childhood but can become perilous in adulthood. The infatuation of an older man often leads to misfortune, giving rise to the adage, "There's no fool like an old fool." Thus, it is advised that older men should not simply fall into love; rather, they ought to approach it with caution. A man in his later years should carefully assess his romantic pursuits, akin to Mr. Barkis’ methodical approach to love.

Mr. Barkis demonstrated a prudent attitude towards the complexities of love when he pondered, "'So she makes,' said Mr. Barkis, after a long interval of reflection, 'all the apple parsties, and does all the cooking, do she?'" To which I confirmed this fact. He continued, "'Well, I'll tell you what,' said Mr. Barkis. 'P'raps you might be writin' to her?'" I assured him that I would indeed write. In response, he thoughtfully remarked, "'Ah!' he said, slowly turning his eyes towards me. 'Well! If you was writin' to her, p'raps you'd recollect to say that Barkis was willin', would you?'"

This exchange exemplifies a careful and measured approach to the realm of middle-aged courtship. The error made by the "Northern Farmer" lay in applying his cautious mindset to the realm of youth. He advised his son Sammy, who desired to marry a poor parson's daughter, with the words, "Doänt thou marry for munny; but goä wheer munny is." In doing so, he presented his own romantic history as a model for Sammy's aspirations.

He recounted, "And I went wheer munny wor, and thy moother coom to and Wi' lots o' munny laäid by, and a nicetish bit o' land. Maybe she worn'd a beauty: I nivver giv' it a thowt; But worn'd she as good to cuddle and kiss as a lass as an't nowt?" 

I’ve always hoped that Sammy chose to disregard his father's advice and pursued his love for the poor parson's daughter instead."
